prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPY whenever it crosses below its 200-day moving average, over the past five years.
why: The supported shape, stated unambiguously: one priceable instrument, a stated window, a stated averaging period, a crossing rule this build executes. It must save, produce figures, carry a reconciled ledger and reopen from stored provenance without another model call.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SP500 ETF every time the S&P 500 crosses below its 200-day moving average for the past 5 years. What would the total amount and return be now?
why: The plan that started this. Must ask which instrument 'SP500 ETF' means, whether 'crosses below' fires once per drawdown or on every day below, and then execute — reporting more than one purchase. A single $1,000 contribution is the original defect.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPY every day the S&P 500 trades under its 200-day moving average, for the past 5 years.
why: The other reading of the same rule. 'Every day under' must produce many more purchases than 'crosses below', and a far larger total contributed. If the two produce the same number the distinction the compiler asks about is not reaching the engine.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of VOO every time it crosses below its moving average, over the past 5 years.
why: No averaging window stated. A 50-session and a 200-session average are different rules; the product must ask rather than assume 200.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPX every time it crosses below its 200-day moving average, for the past 5 years.
why: SPX is the index, not a tradeable fund. The product must say so and offer priceable instruments — and must not silently rewrite SPX to SPY, which would answer a question the user did not ask.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPY at the same day's close whenever it crosses below its 200-day moving average, past 5 years.
why: Trading the close that produced the signal reads one bar into the future. The engine supports next-session execution only and must decline rather than quietly substituting it.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPY every time it crosses below its 200-day moving average, over the past 3 months.
why: A window shorter than the 200-session warm-up. Either no crossing can be evaluated at all, or the result rests on a handful of events. Whatever it does, it must not report a confident return from zero purchases.

prompt: Every time SPY crosses below its 200-day moving average I put in $1,000, and I also invest $500 every month, for the past 5 years.
why: Both funding modes at once. The scenario model holds one funding policy, so this is either refused or one half is silently dropped — and a dropped half is the original defect wearing different clothes. This is the sharpest probe here.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPY every time it crosses below its 200-day moving average and sell everything when it crosses back above, for the past 5 years.
why: A sell leg. Nothing in this build executes an exit condition, so the plan must either refuse or state plainly that the sell was not modelled. A figure with no such statement would be a result for a different strategy.

prompt: I buy £1,000 of SPY every time it crosses below its 200-day moving average, past 5 years.
why: A currency the engine does not model. Reading £ as $ would be a silent 25% error in the contribution.

prompt: I put $2,000 a year into VTI and hold it. Past 5 years.
why: Simplest possible plan. If this needs more than a couple of questions, the clarification loop is too eager.

prompt: I invest $250 in VTI every week for the past 5 years.
why: Weekly dollar-cost averaging — a scheduled funding policy, the counterpart to the event-triggered one.

prompt: I hold 60% VTI and 40% BND and rebalance once a year, past 5 years, starting with $50,000.
why: Rebalancing requires selling. 'equal weight maintained' plus 'never sell' is a contradiction the compiler already detects; this checks that an explicit rebalance is either executed or declared unmodelled.

prompt: I put $1,000 a month into a value tilt using VTV alongside VTI, past 5 years.
why: Two instruments with an implied weighting nobody stated.

prompt: Allocate $100,000 across VTI, BND and GLD by inverse volatility, rebalanced monthly, past 5 years.
why: An allocation rule computed from the data. Not something this build's weighting model expresses.

prompt: I buy $1,000 split equally across AMZN, META, GOOGL, ORCL, AAPL and NVDA every day SPY is below its 200-day moving average, past 5 years.
why: The workbook's own version of the pilot user's rule, with a six-name basket. Tests that the watched series and the bought basket stay distinct — and none of those six is priceable in the synthetic snapshot, so a data-gap refusal is correct.

prompt: I buy $1,000 of SPY only on the day it crosses below its 200-day moving average, past 5 years.
why: The crossing-event reading, stated unambiguously. Should need no trigger question at all.

prompt: I hold SPY while it is above its 10-month simple moving average and switch to Treasury bills when it is below, checked at each month end, past 5 years.
why: A switching rule with an exit leg and a monthly evaluation cadence. Out of scope; must say so.

prompt: Each month I hold whichever of US stocks, international stocks or bonds had the best 12-month return, past 5 years.
why: Dual momentum. Requires ranking on a lookback the engine does not compute.

prompt: I buy SPY when its 50-day average crosses above its 200-day average and sell when it crosses below, past 5 years.
why: Two moving averages and a sell leg. The signal abstraction supports one series against its own average.

prompt: I invest $1,000 a month into VTI, but only in months when VTI is above its 200-day moving average, past 5 years.
why: A schedule *filtered* by a condition — genuinely a third funding shape, neither purely scheduled nor purely triggered. The most interesting catalogue row for the funding model.

prompt: I invest $1,000 a month into VTI and double it in any month after the market falls more than 20%, past 5 years.
why: A conditional amount rather than a conditional purchase.

prompt: I buy SPY when it is above its 200-day average and volatility is low, otherwise hold cash, weekly, past 5 years.
why: A two-factor condition including a volatility measure.

prompt: Each month I sell any of VTI or ITOT that is down and buy the other to keep my exposure, past 5 years.
why: Tax-loss harvesting with a wash-sale dimension. Not modelled, and a figure here would imply a tax benefit nobody computed.

prompt: I hold the 500 largest US companies individually rather than through an ETF, contributing $5,000 a quarter, past 5 years.
why: Direct indexing. Hundreds of instruments, none priceable here.

prompt: I keep bonds in my traditional IRA and stocks in my taxable account, $2,000 a month total, past 5 years.
why: Asset location across two accounts. One plan models one account treatment.

prompt: Convert enough of my traditional IRA to a Roth each year to fill the 12% bracket, past 5 years.
why: Roth conversion. Requires bracket arithmetic and income the engine has no model for.

prompt: I withdraw 4% of my $1,000,000 portfolio in the first year and increase it with inflation each year after, past 5 years.
why: Withdrawals rather than contributions — a negative flow. The schedule model has withdrawals; whether the builder reaches them is the question.

prompt: I contribute enough to my 401(k) to get the full employer match, then the rest to an IRA, $2,000 a month, past 5 years.
why: Employer match is explicitly not modelled.

prompt: I take my required minimum distribution from my IRA each year starting at age 73, past 5 years.
why: RMD tables and age. No model for either.

prompt: My RSUs vest quarterly and I sell them all immediately and buy VTI, past 5 years.
why: RSU is recognised and refused by design — the route returns 501 rather than misreading a vest as cash arriving.

prompt: I put $1,000 a month toward my credit card at 22% instead of investing it, past 5 years.
why: Debt payoff. There is no liability model, and comparing it to investing would imply one.

prompt: I give $10,000 to charity each year from my portfolio, past 5 years.
why: A recurring withdrawal with a tax story attached. The withdrawal may model; the deduction must not silently appear.

prompt: I hold national municipal bonds instead of taxable bonds, $100,000, past 5 years.
why: Municipal tax treatment. Not modelled, and the entire point of the strategy is the tax treatment.

prompt: I keep three months of expenses in cash and invest the rest, $5,000 a month, past 5 years.
why: A cash reserve alongside investing. Cash policy exists; 'three months of expenses' is not a figure the engine holds.
